## _Outline_

::: {.incremental}

* Why items need to be rated by an expert panel before piloting
* Assembling the panel: who counts as an expert, and how many
* The relevance rating form and how to send it out
* Computing **I-CVI** and **S-CVI**, and why the two can give different impressions
* Correcting for **agreement that occurs by chance**
* What to do with items that do not pass
* What the CVI cannot tell you

:::

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}

* **Session 9** produced the construct specification: definition, boundary, estimand, facets, and indicators.

* **Session 10** produced the blueprint and the item list, with a response format.

* **Today** that item list is judged by other people, before any respondent completes it.

:::

::: {.notes}
Brief introduction if this is the first session with this class. Check that every group has brought
its construct specification and item list. Groups without them cannot fully take part in today's
practical work; have them complete it during this session.
:::

## How this connects to what came before

::: {.incremental}

* In **Session 7**, validity was treated as a body of evidence rather than a single number. One source of that evidence is **test content**.

* The CVI is a way of making content evidence **computable and reportable**.

:::

# Assembling the panel {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Who counts as an expert

::: {.incremental}

* **Content experts** — people who know the construct: lecturers, researchers, or practitioners in the field.

* **Method experts** — people who know scale construction and can judge whether an item is well written.

* **Representatives of the target population** — people whose characteristics resemble those of your respondents.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
These three give different kinds of feedback. A panel made up entirely of academics tends to miss readability problems that a prospective respondent spots immediately.
:::

## How many

::: {.incremental}

* **At least 3.** Below that, agreement means very little.

* **5 to 10** is the usual and safer range.

* The size of the panel determines the pass criterion for each item, so decide the number first.

:::

::: aside
[Lynn (1986).](https://journals.lww.com/nursingresearchonline/_layouts/15/oaks.journals/downloadpdf.aspx?an=00006199-198611000-00017)
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
#### An odd number is more practical
With an even number, agreement can split exactly down the middle, leaving you with no basis for a decision.
:::

::: {.notes}
For a one-semester project, 3–5 raters is realistic: a lecturer from a related course, a postgraduate
student, and one or two representatives of the target population. Stress that with a small panel the
criterion is actually stricter — every rater must agree.
:::

## What to send the panel

::: {.incremental}

1. The **construct definition** from Session 9, including the construct boundary.
2. The **blueprint**, so raters can see which facet each item is meant to represent.
3. The **item list**, clearly numbered.
4. The **rating form** with its instructions.
5. A clear **deadline**.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
#### The most commonly forgotten item
Sending the item list **without the construct definition**. Raters then judge relevance against their own understanding of the construct — and the result cannot be interpreted.
:::

# The rating form {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## A four-point relevance scale

| Rating | Meaning |
|:--:|---|
| 1 | Not relevant |
| 2 | Somewhat relevant, needs major revision |
| 3 | Quite relevant, needs minor revision |
| 4 | Highly relevant |

::: aside
Waltz & Bausell (1981); Davis (1992).
:::

. . .

::: {.incremental}

* Four points, **with no midpoint**. Raters have to commit: relevant or not.

* For the computation, ratings of **3 and 4** count as "relevant"; **1 and 2** count as "not relevant".

:::

## Add these two things

::: {.incremental}

* **A comment box** for each item. A number alone does not tell you what to fix.

* **One question at the end**: *"Is there any important aspect of this construct that the items above do not cover?"*

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Why that last question matters
The CVI only checks whether the items that **exist** are relevant. It cannot check whether part of the construct is **not covered at all**.

That is construct underrepresentation from Session 7. The only way to check it through a panel is to ask directly.
:::

# Computing the I-CVI {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Download the Excel template for computing the CVI

::: {.incremental}

* We provide an Excel template for computing I-CVI, S-CVI Universal Agreement (UA), S-CVI Average (Ave), and the chance-corrected modified kappa (κ*).

* These concepts are explained in the next few slides.

:::

. . .

### [Click here to download the template](libs/menghitung-icvi.xlsx)


## The formula

$$\text{I-CVI} = \frac{\text{number of raters giving a 3 or 4}}{\text{total number of raters}}$$

. . .

::: {.incremental}

* Computed **for each item**, one value per item.

* It ranges from 0 to 1.

* Example: of 6 raters, 5 give a 3 or 4. Then I-CVI = 5/6 = **0.83**.

:::

## An example: 8 items, 6 raters

| Item | Raters judging it relevant | I-CVI |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A1 | 6 | 1.00 |
| A2 | 6 | 1.00 |
| A3 | 5 | 0.83 |
| A4 | 6 | 1.00 |
| A5 | 4 | 0.67 |
| A6 | 5 | 0.83 |
| A7 | 6 | 1.00 |
| A8 | 3 | 0.50 |

::: {.notes}
Have students compute the I-CVI column themselves before showing it. It is quick and it makes the
formula stick. Ask which items they think are problematic before introducing the criteria.
:::

## The pass criteria

::: {.incremental}

* With **3 to 5 raters**: I-CVI must be **1.00**. Every rater must agree.

* With **6 to 8 raters**: I-CVI must be at least **0.83**.

* With **9 or more raters**: I-CVI must be at least **0.78**.

:::

::: aside
Lynn (1986); Polit & Beck (2006).
:::

. . .

In the example above, with 6 raters, two items fail: **A5** (0.67) and **A8** (0.50).

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
Note that the criterion is **stricter when there are fewer raters**. The reason is on the next slide.
:::

# Agreement by chance {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## The problem

::: {.incremental}

* If raters answered at random, some agreement would still appear **by chance**.

* With few raters, that chance is substantial. With 3 raters, the probability that all three happen to rate an item "relevant" is 12.5%.

* So I-CVI on its own can look better than it should.

:::

## Modified kappa

The probability of chance agreement:

$$p_c = \binom{N}{A} \times 0.5^N$$

Then:

$$\kappa^* = \frac{\text{I-CVI} - p_c}{1 - p_c}$$

where $N$ is the number of raters and $A$ the number judging the item relevant.

::: aside
Polit, Beck, & Owen (2007).
:::

## Applied to the example

| Item | $A$ | I-CVI | $p_c$ | $\kappa^*$ | Verdict |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|---|
| A1 | 6 | 1.00 | 0.016 | 1.00 | excellent |
| A3 | 5 | 0.83 | 0.094 | 0.82 | excellent |
| A5 | 4 | 0.67 | 0.234 | 0.56 | fair |
| A8 | 3 | 0.50 | 0.313 | 0.27 | poor |

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
The usual benchmarks: $\kappa^* > 0.74$ excellent, $0.60$–$0.74$ good, $0.40$–$0.59$ fair, below that poor.

Note A8: an I-CVI of 0.50 looks like "half agreed", but once corrected, the agreement is barely better than guessing.
:::

# Computing the S-CVI {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Two methods, two numbers

::: {.incremental}

* **S-CVI/Ave** — the average of all the I-CVIs. It describes average relevance.

* **S-CVI/UA** — the proportion of items on which **all** raters agreed (universal agreement). Considerably stricter.

:::

. . .

For the example above:

$$\text{S-CVI/Ave} = \frac{6.83}{8} = 0.85 \qquad \text{S-CVI/UA} = \frac{4}{8} = 0.50$$

## Same data, different impression

::: {.r-fit-text}
0.85 looks adequate.

0.50 looks poor.
:::

<br>

. . .

::: {.incremental}

* Both come from exactly the same table.

* Polit & Beck (2006) wrote a paper specifically about this confusion: many reports cite "the CVI" without saying which one.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
#### What your group must do
State **explicitly** which computation you used. Writing "CVI = 0.85" without qualification leaves the number uninterpretable.

The one usually reported is **S-CVI/Ave**, with a benchmark of at least **0.90**.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most common error in student reports. Stress that both are legitimate as long as the
method is named. If time allows, have one group compute both figures from their own data and
compare them.
:::

# What comes next {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Items that do not pass

::: {.incremental}

* **Revise first, do not delete straight away.** Read the raters' comments. The problem is often the wording rather than the idea.

* **Delete** if the item really measures something else, or if the facet is already better represented by another item.

* **Keep it with a stated reason** if it is conceptually essential and has no replacement. Write that reason into the report.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
Recall the attenuation paradox from Session 7. Dropping items purely to produce tidier numbers can narrow content coverage, which does more harm than good.
:::

## Recompute after revision

If A5 and A8 are revised and re-rated, or removed:

::: {.incremental}

* The six remaining items have I-CVIs of 1.00, 1.00, 0.83, 1.00, 0.83, and 1.00

* $\text{S-CVI/Ave} = 5.67 / 6 = \mathbf{0.94}$

* That now passes the 0.90 benchmark.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
Report **both**: the result before revision and after, together with the decision taken on each item. What is assessed is the process, not only the final number.
:::

# What the CVI cannot do {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Three things it does not check

::: {.incremental}

* **Completeness.** The CVI judges the items that exist, not the items that should exist. For that you have to ask the panel directly.

* **Clarity for respondents.** Expert raters read items differently from prospective respondents. Clarity is checked through cognitive interviewing, as covered in Session 7.

* **Whether the construct itself makes sense.** If your construct definition is flawed, the panel will rate relevance against that flawed definition.

:::

::: aside
[Haynes, Richard, & Kubany (1995)](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1996-03400-001); [Rubio et al. (2003)](https://academic.oup.com/swr/article-abstract/27/2/94/1659075).
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
The CVI is one source of evidence. It occupies one row of the validity evidence table from Session 7.
:::

# Practical work {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Part 1: preparing the panel pack

**30 minutes.** Each group prepares:

::: {.incremental}

1. The pack for raters: construct definition, blueprint, numbered item list.
2. A rating form with the 4-point scale, comment boxes, and the completeness question.
3. A list of prospective raters and their role: content expert, method expert, or population representative.
4. A return deadline.

:::

::: {.notes}
Circulate and check that the construct definition is actually included — this is the step most often
missed. Check too that item numbering is consistent with the blueprint.
If possible, encourage each group to send the pack to raters by the end of this week, so responses
are back before the pilot in Session 12.
:::

## Part 2: practising the computation

**25 minutes.** Groups swap and act as raters for one another.

::: {.incremental}

* Each group member rates **10 items belonging to another group** using the 4-point scale.

* Collect the ratings and compute: **I-CVI for each item**, **$\kappa^*$**, and both **S-CVI/Ave** and **S-CVI/UA**.

* Identify which items fail, and write one revision suggestion for each.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
This exercise uses classmates as raters, so the result is not genuine validity evidence. The point is to make sure the computation is correct before the real panel data arrives.
:::

::: {.notes}
The computation can be done on paper or in a spreadsheet. The most frequent mistakes: forgetting
that ratings of 3 and 4 both count as relevant, and confusing S-CVI/Ave with S-CVI/UA.
Leave 15 minutes to work through one or two groups' results with the whole class.
:::

## What you must produce

::: {.incremental}

* A **panel pack** ready to send.
* A **computation table** with I-CVI, $\kappa^*$, S-CVI/Ave, and S-CVI/UA.
* A **decision record** for each item: kept, revised, or removed, with the reason.
* A **revised item list**, ready for the pilot.

:::

## For Session 12

::: {.incremental}

* Designing the **pilot study**: who the respondents are, how many, and how to reach them.
* Setting data-cleaning rules **before** the data arrives.
* Including **one short comparison scale** for evidence on relations to other variables.
* Running short cognitive interviews with 3–5 people before distributing the questionnaire.

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Preparation
Bring today's revised item list. If ratings from your actual panel have come back, bring those too.
:::
